questions.question: ______ is a severe manifestation of protein-energy malnutrition that occurs as a result of total calorie insufficiency.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Marasmus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Marasmus** is a severe form of protein-energy malnutrition resulting from a **total calorie insufficiency**. It occurs due to prolonged starvation, inadequate nutrition, or lack of food intake.
 
• This condition leads to **extreme wasting of body tissues**, including muscles and fat, resulting in emaciation and very low body weight.
 
• Children suffering from marasmus exhibit symptoms like **stunted growth, weak immunity, dry skin, brittle hair, and sunken eyes**.
 
• Marasmus is typically observed in **infants and young children**, especially in regions with widespread poverty or famine.
 
• The condition can be prevented and treated through **adequate nutritional interventions**, including a balanced diet rich in proteins, carbohydrates, and essential vitamins and minerals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Protein-Energy Malnutrition (PEM):**

 
 
• PEM refers to a range of malnutrition disorders caused by **insufficient intake of protein and calories**. Marasmus is one of the most severe forms of PEM.
 
• It often occurs in areas with **food scarcity, inadequate healthcare, and poor sanitation**.
 
 
 
• **Kwashiorkor:**
 
 
• Kwashiorkor is another form of protein-energy malnutrition, caused specifically by a **deficiency of protein** while calorie intake may be adequate.
 
• It is characterized by **edema (swelling), irritability, skin lesions, and an enlarged liver**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison Between Marasmus and Kwashiorkor:**
 
 
• Marasmus is due to **total calorie deficit**, while Kwashiorkor is specifically due to **protein deficiency**.
 
• Marasmus results in **extreme thinness**, while Kwashiorkor leads to **swelling and fluid retention**.
 
 
 
• **Preventive Measures:**
 
 
• **Balanced diet:** Ensure a diet rich in proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins, and minerals.
 
• Promote **breastfeeding** in infants for early nutritional security.
 
• Implementing community-based nutritional programs in **poverty-stricken areas**.
 
 
 
• **Other Options:**
 
 
• **Polio:** A viral disease affecting the nervous system, not related to malnutrition.
 
• **Herpes:** A viral infection causing sores, unrelated to nutritional deficiencies.
 
• **Goitre:** Caused by iodine deficiency, leading to thyroid gland enlargement.

questions.question: Who among the following was elected as the Permanent Chairman of the Constituent Assembly in 1946?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dr. Rajendra Prasad**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Dr. Rajendra Prasad** was elected as the **Permanent Chairman** of the **Constituent Assembly** in **1946**. This position was crucial in steering the discussions and drafting the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Constituent Assembly was formed in **December 1946** under the Cabinet Mission Plan to draft the Constitution of India after independence.
 
• Dr. Sachchidananda Sinha served as the **Provisional Chairman** of the Constituent Assembly before Dr. Rajendra Prasad was elected as the Permanent Chairman.
 
• Dr. Rajendra Prasad’s leadership in the Assembly was instrumental in the successful drafting of the **Constitution of India**, which was adopted on **26 November 1949**.
 
• Dr. Rajendra Prasad later went on to become the first **President of India** in **1950**, serving two terms in office.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About the Constituent Assembly:**

 
 
• The Constituent Assembly was established under the recommendations of the **Cabinet Mission Plan** in **1946**.
 
• It consisted of **389 members**, out of which **292** were elected by provincial legislatures, **93** represented princely states, and **4** represented the Chief Commissioners' provinces.
 
• The Assembly was responsible for drafting the Constitution of India and held its first session on **9 December 1946**.
 
• The Constitution was adopted on **26 November 1949** and came into effect on **26 January 1950**.
 
 
 
• **Role of Dr. Rajendra Prasad:**
 
 
• Dr. Rajendra Prasad was a prominent leader of the Indian National Congress and played a significant role in the **freedom movement**.
 
• He was known for his ability to maintain harmony and facilitate discussions among the diverse members of the Assembly.
 
• His presidency of the Constituent Assembly reflected his stature as a statesman and his commitment to creating a democratic framework for India.
 
 
 
• **Other Key Members of the Constituent Assembly:**
 
 
• **Jawaharlal Nehru:** Presented the Objectives Resolution, which laid the foundation of the Constitution.
 
• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar:** Served as the Chairman of the Drafting Committee, playing a pivotal role in drafting the Constitution.
 
• **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel:** Played a significant role in integrating princely states into India.
 
• **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad:** Contributed to debates on cultural and religious rights.
 
 
 
• **Important Developments in the Constituent Assembly:**
 
 
• The **Objectives Resolution**, moved by Jawaharlal Nehru on **13 December 1946**, outlined the philosophy and goals of the Constitution.
 
• The Drafting Committee, chaired by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, submitted the draft Constitution, which was debated and finalized by the Assembly.
 
• The Constitution was signed by the members of the Assembly on **24 January 1950**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The Constituent Assembly functioned as the **Provisional Parliament** of India from **26 January 1950** until the first general elections in **1952**.
 
• The Assembly took **2 years, 11 months, and 18 days** to complete the drafting of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Constitution of India is the **longest written Constitution** in the world, with **395 Articles** (at the time of adoption) divided into **22 Parts** and **8 Schedules**.
 
• The Constituent Assembly sessions were held in the Central Hall of Parliament House in New Delhi.

questions.question: The Central Reserve Police Force is governed by the CRPF Act. In which of the following years was the CRPF Act enacted after independence?

__
 
• The **Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) Act** was enacted in **1949**, two years after India achieved independence. This act provides the legislative framework for the functioning of the CRPF.
 
• The CRPF was initially constituted as the **Crown Representative’s Police** in **1939** during British rule and was later reorganized under the CRPF Act, 1949.
 
• The primary role of the CRPF is to ensure **internal security and maintenance of law and order** in the country. It operates under the authority of the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.
 
• The CRPF Act, 1949, defines the structure, duties, powers, and responsibilities of the force, making it the largest paramilitary organization in India.

__
 
• **Historical Background of CRPF:**

 
 
• The CRPF originated as the **Crown Representative’s Police** in **1939**, tasked with protecting British interests in India.
 
• After independence, the force was restructured to align with India's democratic framework and renamed the **Central Reserve Police Force**.
 
• The CRPF Act, 1949, formalized this transition and outlined its operational mandate.
 
 
 
• **Roles and Responsibilities:**
 
 
• The CRPF is primarily responsible for maintaining **internal security**, controlling riots, and addressing insurgency in various parts of India.
 
• It also plays a key role in **VIP security**, election security, and disaster response.
 
• The force operates specialized units such as the Rapid Action Force (RAF) for riot control and the Commando Battalion for Resolute Action (COBRA) for anti-Naxalite operations.
 
 
 
• **Significant Contributions:**

• It has been involved in **United Nations peacekeeping missions** globally, showcasing its capability to operate internationally.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Options:**
 
 
• **1952:** This year is incorrect, as the CRPF Act was already enacted in 1949.
 
• **1948:** Although close to the correct year, the CRPF Act was enacted after this in 1949.
 
• **1949:** Correct year of enactment, marking the establishment of the CRPF under Indian law.
 
• **1956:** Incorrect year, as it is unrelated to the enactment of the CRPF Act.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Ministry of Home Affairs:** The CRPF operates directly under the Ministry of Home Affairs, ensuring its integration into India's overall internal security strategy.

__
 
• **Shevaroy Hills** are located in the state of **Tamil Nadu**, specifically in the **Salem district**.
 
• The Shevaroy Hills form part of the **Eastern Ghats**, a mountain range that runs parallel to India's eastern coast.
 
• These hills are known for their **pleasant climate** and serve as a famous hill station, with **Yercaud** being the most prominent destination.
 
• The Shevaroy Hills are primarily covered with forests and plantations, including coffee, spices, and orange cultivation, contributing to the local economy.
 
• The hills are also home to the **Shevaroy Temple**, dedicated to Lord Shevaroy, which is a popular pilgrimage site for locals.

__
 
• **Eastern Ghats:**

 
 
• The Eastern Ghats are a discontinuous mountain range running along the eastern coast of India, passing through states like Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, and Karnataka.
 
• They are comparatively lower in elevation than the Western Ghats and have been subjected to significant erosion over time.
 
• Some important hill stations located in the Eastern Ghats include **Yercaud** in Tamil Nadu and **Araku Valley** in Andhra Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Yercaud:**
 
 
• Yercaud is a popular hill station in the Shevaroy Hills, situated at an altitude of around **1,515 meters** above sea level.
 
• It is often referred to as the "Poor Man's Ooty" due to its affordability compared to other hill stations like Ooty.
 
• Tourist attractions in Yercaud include the **Yercaud Lake**, **Botanical Garden**, and **Killiyur Waterfalls**.
 
 
 
• **Shevaroy Temple:**
 
 
• The Shevaroy Temple, located at the highest point of the Shevaroy Hills, is dedicated to Lord Shevaroy and Goddess Kaveri.
 
• The temple is carved out of rocks and is considered sacred by the local tribal communities.
 
• It offers panoramic views of the surrounding landscape, making it a must-visit for tourists and devotees alike.
 
 
 
• **Flora and Fauna:**
 
 
• The Shevaroy Hills are rich in biodiversity, with dense forests and plantations of coffee, black pepper, cardamom, and oranges.

questions.question: The Ministers in the Council are appointed by the President on the advice of the:

__
 
• The **Ministers in the Council of Ministers** are appointed by the **President of India**, but this appointment is made based on the advice of the **Prime Minister**__.
 
• As per **Article 75(1)** of the **Indian Constitution**, the **President appoints the Prime Minister**, and on the advice of the Prime Minister, other ministers are appointed.
 
• The **Prime Minister** plays a pivotal role in selecting and recommending names for the Council of Ministers, ensuring their alignment with the ruling party or coalition's policies and goals.
 
• Ministers in the Council are collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha**, and their continued tenure depends on the confidence of the majority in the Lok Sabha.
 
• This system of appointment ensures that the executive branch is closely tied to the legislative branch, maintaining the principle of collective responsibility in parliamentary democracy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Prime Minister of India:**

 
 
• The **Prime Minister** is the **head of the government** and the leader of the Council of Ministers.
 
• The Prime Minister is appointed by the President under **Article 75** of the Constitution, usually the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha.
 
• The Prime Minister acts as a bridge between the President and the Council of Ministers, advising the President on key appointments and decisions.
 
 
 
• **Role of the President in Appointments:**
 
 
• While the **President** formally appoints the **Prime Minister** and other ministers, their role is largely ceremonial in this context, as the appointments are based on parliamentary procedures.
 
• The President exercises their powers based on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers as per **Article 74(1)**.
 
 
 
• **Composition of the Council of Ministers:**
 
 
• The **Council of Ministers** consists of three categories of ministers: **Cabinet Ministers**, **Ministers of State**, and **Deputy Ministers**.
 
• Cabinet Ministers hold the most significant portfolios and play a central role in policymaking and administration.
 
• Ministers of State may have independent charge or assist Cabinet Ministers, while Deputy Ministers assist in specific duties assigned by senior ministers.
 
 
 
• **Collective Responsibility:**
 
 
• The Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha under **Article 75(3)**.
 
• This principle ensures that all ministers support government decisions publicly, even if they privately disagree with them.
 
 
 
• **Articles of the Constitution Related to Ministers:**
 
 
• **Article 74:** Provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister to aid and advise the President.
 
• **Article 75:** Deals with the appointment, tenure, and responsibilities of ministers.
 
• **Article 77:** States that all executive actions of the government are taken in the name of the President.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Prime Minister’s Role in Parliamentary Democracy:**

 
 
• The Prime Minister is the **chief advisor to the President** and the head of the Council of Ministers.
 
• They are responsible for coordinating the work of various ministries and ensuring the smooth functioning of the government.
 
 
 
• **Process of Appointment:**
 
 
• The **Prime Minister** is appointed first, followed by the appointment of other ministers based on their recommendations.
 
• This process ensures that the executive has the confidence of the majority in the Lok Sabha, reflecting the democratic principle of parliamentary majority.
 
 
 
• **Tenure of Ministers:**
 
 
• Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, but this is subject to the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
 
• If the government loses its majority in the Lok Sabha, the Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, must resign.

questions.question: According to which of the following Articles of the Constitution, has the Union Parliament exclusive jurisdiction to make laws on items in the Union List and the State Legislature the exclusive power to make laws on items given in the State List?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 246**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 246** of the **Indian Constitution** defines the distribution of legislative powers between the **Union Parliament** and the **State Legislatures**.
 
• It provides exclusive jurisdiction to the **Union Parliament** to legislate on matters enumerated in the **Union List** and to the **State Legislatures** for matters in the **State List**.
 
• The **Union List** includes subjects of national importance such as defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, and currency, whereas the **State List** covers local and regional matters like police, public health, and agriculture.
 
• The **Concurrent List** allows both the Union and State legislatures to legislate on matters like criminal law, marriage, and bankruptcy, but in case of a conflict, the Union law prevails.
 
• This article is a key component of the federal structure of India, ensuring clear demarcation of powers and responsibilities between the Centre and the States.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union List:**

 
 
• The Union List in the **Seventh Schedule** of the Constitution contains **97 items** over which only the Parliament has exclusive power to legislate.
 
• Examples include **defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, banking, and communication.**
 
• Matters in this list require national-level uniformity, justifying central control.
 
 
 
• **State List:**
 
 
• The State List contains **66 items** under the **Seventh Schedule** and is exclusively under the legislative competence of the State Legislatures.
 
• Examples include **police, public health, agriculture, and local government.**
 
• This list ensures that States can address region-specific and local issues independently.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List:**
 
 
• The Concurrent List comprises **52 items** shared by both the Union and State Legislatures.
 
• Examples include **criminal law, marriage, education, and bankruptcy.**
 
• In case of a conflict, the law made by the Parliament takes precedence as per Article 254.
 
 
 
• **Article 352:**
 
 
• This article deals with the **Proclamation of Emergency** in case of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.
 
• It does not relate to the division of legislative powers; hence, it is an incorrect option in the context of this question.
 
 
 
• **Article 123:**
 
 
• It grants the **President of India** the power to promulgate ordinances when the Parliament is not in session.
 
• It is unrelated to the legislative powers of the Union and State and is not relevant to this question.
 
 
 
• **Article 234:**
 
 
• This article deals with the control of subordinate judiciary by the High Courts and is unrelated to legislative jurisdiction.
 
• Hence, it is not the correct answer in the context of Union and State legislative powers.

• The **Sabarimala Sree Dharma Sastha Temple** is situated in the state of **Kerala**, India.

• **Festivals and Celebrations:**
 
 
• The temple's main festivals include **Makaravilakku** (celebrated in January) and **Mandala Pooja** (celebrated in December).

• The temple remains closed for most of the year and opens only for specific days and occasions.

• The budget focused on addressing the economic challenges faced by British India after the **1857 Revolt**, which had strained financial resources.

questions.question: The study of the chemistry, crystal structure and physical properties of the mineral constituents of rocks is called ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**mineralogy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mineralogy** is the branch of geology that focuses on the study of the **chemical composition, physical properties, and crystal structure of minerals**, which are the natural building blocks of rocks.
 
• This discipline involves the analysis of **mineral formation, classification, and properties**, as well as their occurrence in nature.
 
• Mineralogists utilize a variety of techniques, such as **microscopic analysis, X-ray diffraction, and spectroscopy**, to identify and study minerals.
 
• The understanding of minerals is essential for several industries, including **mining, construction, and material science**, as well as for environmental and planetary studies.
 
• Mineralogy also contributes to understanding the **geological history of Earth**, as minerals carry information about the conditions under which they formed.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Palaeontology**:

 
 
• This branch of geology deals with the **study of fossils** to understand the history of life on Earth.
 
• Palaeontologists study the remains of **plants, animals, and microorganisms** preserved in rocks to reconstruct past ecosystems and evolutionary processes.
 
 
 
• **Petrology**:
 
 
• Petrology focuses on the study of **rocks**, their composition, origin, and structure.
 
• It is divided into three main sub-disciplines: **igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic petrology**, based on the types of rocks studied.
 
 
 
• **Cryosphere**:
 
 
• The cryosphere refers to the **frozen water part of the Earth system**, including glaciers, ice caps, sea ice, and permafrost.
 
• It plays a significant role in regulating the Earth’s **climate and sea levels**.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Mineralogy**:
 
 
• Mineralogy is crucial in the **mining industry** for identifying and extracting valuable minerals.
 
• It also aids in the development of materials like **ceramics, glass, and semiconductors**.
 
• In planetary science, mineralogy helps in understanding the composition of other celestial bodies, such as the Moon and Mars.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Importance of Mineralogy in Geology**:

 
 
• Understanding the properties of minerals helps geologists determine the **formation conditions of rocks** and geological processes.
 
• Minerals also serve as indicators of **ore deposits**, which are vital for economic geology.
 
 
 
• **Interdisciplinary Significance**:
 
 
• Mineralogy intersects with chemistry, physics, and materials science, contributing to the development of **new materials and technologies**.
 
• It also has applications in **archaeology and art conservation** for identifying pigments and materials used historically.

• It established a system where the **Board of Control**, a body appointed by the British government, would oversee the activities of the East India Company.
 
• The act created a dual system of governance by dividing powers between the **Board of Control** (responsible for political affairs) and the **Court of Directors** of the East India Company (responsible for commercial activities).
 
• It marked a significant step in increasing the British Crown's control over Indian territories, as the Board of Control had the power to guide and supervise the Company's administration in India.

__
 
• **Regulating Act of 1773:**

 
 
• This was the first attempt by the British Parliament to regulate the East India Company's affairs in India.
 
• It established the office of the **Governor-General of Bengal** and a Supreme Court in Calcutta.
 
• However, it lacked provisions for effective control over the Company's administration, leading to the need for Pitt's India Act.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of Pitt's India Act:**
 
 
• It distinguished between the **political** and **commercial** functions of the East India Company.
 
• The British government established the **Board of Control**, which had six members, including the British Chancellor of the Exchequer and the Secretary of State.
 
• The Governor-General in Bengal was given greater authority over the presidencies of Bombay and Madras in matters of governance and military activities.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Act:**
 
 
• The act laid the foundation for the gradual centralization of British administration in India.
 
• It ensured that the British Crown exercised direct oversight over the East India Company's policies in India, particularly in political matters.
 
 
 
• **Subsequent Developments:**
 
 
• The **Charter Act of 1813**, the **Government of India Act of 1858**, and other legislative measures further developed the structure of British administration in India.
 
• Each subsequent act increased the British Crown's authority over Indian governance, leading to the eventual dissolution of the East India Company's role in 1858.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

questions.question: Which of the following is the most abundant element in the universe?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Hydrogen**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hydrogen** is the most abundant element in the universe, making up approximately **75% of the universe's baryonic mass**.
 
• It is primarily found in stars, including our Sun, where it undergoes **nuclear fusion** to form helium and release enormous amounts of energy.
 
• Hydrogen is the simplest and lightest element, with **one proton and one electron**, making it the basic building block of all matter.
 
• This element is present in various forms, including atomic hydrogen, molecular hydrogen (H₂), and ions in the interstellar medium.
 
• Hydrogen is essential in the formation of galaxies, stars, and planets, and plays a crucial role in the chemical composition of the universe. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Elemental Abundance in the Universe:**

 
 
• **Hydrogen:** Comprises approximately **90% of all atoms** and 75% of the universe's mass. Found predominantly in stars and interstellar gases.
 
• **Helium:** The second most abundant element, making up about **24% of the universe's mass**. It is formed through hydrogen fusion in stars.
 
• **Oxygen:** While abundant on Earth, oxygen ranks much lower in the universe's abundance. It is primarily formed in the cores of massive stars.
 
• **Carbon:** Essential for life, carbon is formed during the later stages of stellar evolution and is less abundant compared to hydrogen and helium.
 
• **Nitrogen:** Another element formed in stars, it is vital for life but is far less common in the universe compared to hydrogen and helium.
 
 
 
• **Key Properties of Hydrogen:**
 
 
• **Simplest Element:** Composed of just one proton and one electron, hydrogen is the foundation for the creation of heavier elements.
 
• **Energy Source:** Hydrogen fusion powers stars, including the Sun, through the process of converting hydrogen to helium.
 
• **Forms:** Exists as atomic hydrogen, molecular hydrogen (H₂), and in ionic states in different environments.
 
• **Role in Chemistry:** Hydrogen is a major component of water (H₂O) and organic compounds, essential for life on Earth.
 
 
 
• **Hydrogen in Astronomy:**
 
 
• **Interstellar Medium:** Hydrogen exists as clouds of gas and dust, forming stars and planets over time.
 
• **Galactic Formation:** Hydrogen plays a critical role in the formation of galaxies and nebulae.
 
• **Detection:** Astronomers detect hydrogen using its characteristic emission and absorption lines in the electromagnetic spectrum.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Hydrogen on Earth:**
 
 
• **Fuel:** Hydrogen is used in fuel cells to generate clean energy, producing only water as a byproduct.
 
• **Industry:** Used in processes like ammonia production for fertilizers, refining petroleum, and hydrogenation of oils.
 
• **Space Exploration:** Liquid hydrogen is a key fuel for rockets and spacecraft.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Hydrogen Fusion:**

 
 
• This process occurs in stars, where four hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium, releasing energy.
 
• The Sun converts approximately **600 million tons of hydrogen** into helium every second. 
 
 
 
• **Cosmic Evolution:**
 
 
• Hydrogen was the first element formed after the Big Bang, approximately **13.8 billion years ago**.
 
• Its abundance and simplicity make it crucial for the creation of all other elements through stellar nucleosynthesis.
 
 
 
• **Scientific Significance:**
 
 
• Hydrogen is studied extensively in astrophysics and chemistry to understand the universe's origin and composition.
 
• It serves as a model for quantum mechanics due to its simple atomic structure.

questions.question: UTR (Unique Transaction Reference) is a ______ character code used to uniquely identify a transaction in RTGS system.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**22**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **UTR (Unique Transaction Reference)** is a **22-character alphanumeric code** used in the **RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement)** system to uniquely identify a transaction.
 
• This code serves as a unique identifier for tracking and referencing individual transactions.
 
• The **22-character format** includes details such as the bank code, date of transaction, and unique transaction number, ensuring no two transactions have the same UTR.
 
• It is primarily used in the **RTGS system**, which facilitates high-value and time-critical fund transfers in India.
 
• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** has mandated the use of UTR for all RTGS transactions for better tracking and resolution of disputes.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **What is RTGS?**

 
 
• **RTGS** stands for **Real Time Gross Settlement**, a system where fund transfers are processed in real-time and on a gross basis.
 
• It is intended for **high-value transactions**, with a minimum transfer amount of **₹2,00,000** and no upper limit.
 
• RTGS is managed by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and operates on a secure platform.
 
• Transactions in RTGS are final and irrevocable.
 
 
 
• **Structure of UTR:**
 
 
• The **22-character UTR** is structured as follows:
 
 
• The first four characters represent the **bank code**.
 
• The next six characters indicate the **date of transaction**.
 
• The remaining twelve characters are a **unique transaction number**.
 
 
 
• For example, a UTR might look like **SBINH0123456789012345**, where "SBIN" is the bank code for the State Bank of India.
 
 
 
• **Uses of UTR:**
 
 
• It helps in **tracking the status of RTGS transactions**.
 
• It ensures quick resolution of disputes or issues related to failed or delayed transactions.
 
• UTR is used by banks and customers alike for **transaction reconciliation**.
 
 
 
• **Difference between RTGS and NEFT:**
 
 
• While **RTGS** processes transactions in real-time and on a gross basis, **NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer)** settles transactions in batches and is more suited for smaller value transactions.
 
• Both systems use a **unique reference number**, but RTGS employs a UTR with a **22-character format**, whereas NEFT uses a unique 16-character reference ID.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• RTGS is available 24x7, making it a convenient option for urgent high-value transfers.
 
• The UTR ensures transparency and traceability in financial transactions.
 
• Both banks and customers should retain the UTR for future reference, especially in cases of payment disputes.

• **Key Features of Nepal's 2015 Constitution:**

 
 
• The 2015 Constitution is the **seventh Constitution** in Nepal's history and the first one drafted by a democratically elected Constituent Assembly.
 
• It contains **308 articles, 35 parts, and 9 schedules**.
 
• The Constitution recognizes Nepal as a **multi-ethnic, multi-lingual, and multi-cultural nation**.
 
• The document ensures a number of fundamental rights, including **freedom of speech, religion, and equality**, along with rights to health and education.
 
• The Constitution reserves **33% representation for women** in Parliament and provides for proportional representation for marginalized communities.
 
 
 
• **Political Background Leading to the Constitution:**
 
 
• Nepal transitioned from a monarchy to a **federal democratic republic** in 2008, following the abolition of the monarchy after a decade-long civil war.

• The **2006 Comprehensive Peace Accord** ended the civil war and initiated the process of drafting a new Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Provinces and Federalism:**
 
 
• The Constitution divides Nepal into **seven provinces**, each with its own legislature and executive powers.
 
• The aim of federalism was to address regional and ethnic disparities by decentralizing power.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Implementation:**
 
 
• The promulgation of the Constitution was met with protests, particularly from the **Madhesi and Tharu communities**, who felt underrepresented in the federal structure.
 
• There were demands for amendments to address concerns related to **citizenship, boundaries, and proportional representation**.

questions.question: In which of the following time periods was the first census conducted in India non-synchronously in different parts?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1865-1872**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The first census in India was conducted non-synchronously** during the period **1865-1872**, meaning it was carried out at different times in different regions.
 
• This census was conducted under the supervision of **British colonial administration** to collect demographic data for administrative and governance purposes.
 
• The census was not conducted simultaneously across the country due to logistical challenges, lack of uniform administrative structures, and varying geographical conditions.
 
• It was during the tenure of **Lord Mayo** (Governor-General of India from 1869 to 1872) that the idea of a systematic census gained momentum.
 
• The census effort culminated in the first synchronous census of India in **1881**, which marked a transition to a more organized and uniform approach.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Historical Background of Census in India:**

 
 
• The idea of a census in India originated during British rule for purposes like taxation, governance, and social reforms.
 
• The first census conducted non-synchronously during **1865-1872** was experimental and lacked standardization.
 
• The first synchronous census took place in **1881**, under the leadership of **W.C. Plowden**, the Census Commissioner of India.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Census:**
 
 
• The census provides vital demographic data on **population size, density, literacy rates, employment, and housing.**
 
• It serves as a critical tool for planning and implementing policies related to health, education, infrastructure, and social welfare.
 
• Census data is used to allocate resources and funds to different states and regions based on population needs.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Early Census:**
 
 
• Non-uniform administrative systems across regions made data collection inconsistent.
 
• Geographical diversity and lack of transportation infrastructure posed logistical difficulties.
 
• Illiteracy and lack of awareness among the population added to the complexity of data collection.
 
 
 
• **Key Developments in Census Post-1881:**
 
 
• The census became a regular exercise, conducted every 10 years.
 
• With advancements in technology and administrative systems, census data collection became more efficient and reliable.
 
• Modern censuses in India include data on gender, religion, languages, migration patterns, and socio-economic indicators.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of Census in India:**

 
 
• India's census is conducted by the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner** under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
 
• The census collects data on various parameters such as **population characteristics, housing, education, employment, and migration.**
 
• The most recent census was conducted in **2011**, and the next census is scheduled to take place after delays caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Census Data:**
 
 
• Census data is crucial for electoral processes, such as determining the number of constituencies based on population.
 
• It aids researchers, policymakers, and planners in analyzing trends and formulating strategies for national development.
 
• The data is used in international comparisons and for understanding demographic transitions over time.

questions.question: The Ilbert Bill Act was introduced by Lord Ripon in which of the following years?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1883**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Ilbert Bill** was introduced by **Lord Ripon**, the Viceroy of India, in the year **1883**.
 
• This bill sought to abolish the judicial inequality between **Indian and European judges** by allowing Indian judges to preside over cases involving European citizens in the criminal courts.
 
• The bill faced intense opposition from the British community in India, who argued that Indian judges lacked the competence and impartiality to handle cases involving Europeans.
 
• The opposition led to widespread protests and debates, culminating in the modification of the bill. The revised version required that cases involving Europeans be tried by a jury with at least half of the members being Europeans.
 
• The controversy surrounding the Ilbert Bill highlighted the deep racial prejudices and discrimination prevalent during British rule in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Ripon:**

 
 
• Lord Ripon served as the **Viceroy of India from 1880 to 1884** and is often regarded as the father of **local self-government in India**.
 
• He implemented several reforms, including the introduction of the **Ilbert Bill**, which was aimed at empowering Indian judges and addressing judicial discrimination.
 
• His tenure also saw the repeal of the controversial **Vernacular Press Act of 1878**, which had restricted the freedom of the Indian press.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Ilbert Bill:**
 
 
• The Ilbert Bill controversy exposed the deep-seated **racial tensions** and prejudices in colonial India.
 
• It also underscored the growing **political awareness** and aspirations of educated Indians, who began demanding greater representation and equality under British rule.
 
• The controversy surrounding the bill is often seen as a precursor to the rise of organized political movements in India, including the formation of the **Indian National Congress in 1885**.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The Ilbert Bill was part of Lord Ripon’s broader efforts to reform and modernize India’s administrative and judicial systems.
 
• It was introduced at a time when Indians were increasingly demanding **equal treatment** and opportunities in the colonial administration.
 
 
 
• **Opposition to the Bill:**
 
 
• The British community in India launched a vigorous campaign against the Ilbert Bill, claiming that it threatened their social and legal privileges.
 
• The bill was ultimately amended to appease the European community, reflecting the limited scope of reforms under colonial rule.

questions.question: What do you call a person who has dependence on any narcotic drug or any psychotropic substance?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Addict**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An **Addict** is defined as a person who has developed a compulsive dependence on a substance, such as a narcotic drug or psychotropic substance, despite harmful consequences.
 
• In the context of substance abuse, addiction involves a **physical and psychological dependence**, making it difficult for the individual to quit the drug or substance voluntarily.
 
• Psychotropic substances refer to drugs that affect the **central nervous system**, altering mood, consciousness, perception, and behavior. Examples include opioids, cannabis, and amphetamines.
 
• While tolerance and dependence are components of addiction, addiction itself is characterized by a **loss of control** and continued usage despite negative consequences.
 
• The term “addict” is often replaced with “individual with substance use disorder” in modern medical terminology to reduce stigma and focus on treatment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tolerant:**

 
 
• Tolerance refers to a person’s reduced sensitivity to a drug over time, requiring higher doses to achieve the same effect.
 
• It is a physiological phenomenon and does not necessarily indicate addiction. For example, a person using painkillers for a medical condition may develop tolerance without being addicted.
 
 
 
• **Dependent:**
 
 
• Dependence refers to a state where the body adapts to a drug, leading to withdrawal symptoms if the drug is stopped abruptly.
 
• It can be physical, characterized by symptoms like nausea and tremors, or psychological, involving intense cravings.
 
 
 
• **Psychotic:**
 
 
• Psychosis is a severe mental disorder characterized by a loss of contact with reality, often involving delusions and hallucinations.
 
• It is not directly related to addiction, although substance abuse can sometimes trigger psychotic episodes in vulnerable individuals.
 
 
 
• **Key Statistics:**
 
 
• According to the **World Drug Report 2023** by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), around **296 million people** globally used drugs in 2021, with many developing addiction.
 
• In India, the **National Survey on Extent and Pattern of Substance Use in India 2019** reported that around **22.6 million people** used opioids, with many falling into addiction.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives in India:**
 
 
• The **National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) (2018-2025)** aims to reduce substance abuse through prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation.
 
• The **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985**, regulates the manufacture, possession, sale, and transport of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances to combat addiction.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jat-Jatin** is a traditional **folk dance** that originates from the state of **Bihar** in India.
 
• This dance is particularly popular in the **Mithila region** of Bihar and is known for its vibrant and expressive performances.
 
• **Jat-Jatin** is typically performed during the **monsoon season** and is closely associated with rural communities.
 
• The dance depicts the **conversations and emotions** between a husband (Jat) and his wife (Jatin), symbolizing their love, longing, and relationship dynamics.
 
• It is often accompanied by **folk songs** that narrate stories of rural life, social issues, or romantic tales, making it a unique cultural expression of the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Folk Dances of Bihar:**

• **Chhau:** A semi-classical dance that combines martial arts and folk traditions; it is popular in Bihar as well as parts of Odisha and West Bengal.
 
• **Sohar-Khilouna:** Performed during childbirth celebrations, this dance reflects joy and gratitude.
 
 
 
• **Features of Jat-Jatin Dance:**
 
 
• This dance involves a **male and female pair**, symbolizing the husband-wife relationship.
 
• The performers wear **traditional attire** that reflects the culture of rural Bihar.
 
• The themes often revolve around **love, separation, and reunion**, portraying human emotions through expressive movements.
 
 
 
• **Cultural Importance:**

• It serves as a medium to **preserve traditional values** and pass them on to future generations.
 
 
 
• **Other Folk Dances in India:**
 
 
• **Bihu:** A dance from Assam performed during the Bihu festival.
 
• **Ghoomar:** A traditional dance of Rajasthan, known for its graceful movements.
 
• **Lavani:** A popular dance form of Maharashtra, characterized by its rhythmic footwork and strong beats.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Jat-Jatin Dance:** It reflects the rural life and social issues of Bihar, making it an integral part of the state's cultural identity.
 
• **Preservation Efforts:** Various cultural organizations and festivals in Bihar promote Jat-Jatin to keep the tradition alive.
 
• **Significance:** This dance is not only a form of entertainment but also a way to address societal themes and foster community bonding.

questions.question: ______ is a slowdown or a massive contraction in economic activities.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Recession**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Recession** refers to a significant decline in economic activity across the economy, lasting for an extended period, typically measured in months or quarters.
 
• It is identified by a decrease in **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**, income levels, employment rates, industrial production, and retail sales.
 
• During a recession, businesses reduce investments, lay off employees, and consumers spend less, leading to a cycle of declining demand and production.
 
• Recessions are often triggered by factors like **financial crises**, high inflation, or major geopolitical events. For example, the **2008 Global Financial Crisis** led to a worldwide recession.
 
• **Indicators** of a recession include rising unemployment rates, declining stock markets, and reduced consumer confidence. These signs reflect reduced economic activity and growth.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Recession Characteristics:**

 
 
• A recession is declared when there are two consecutive quarters of negative **GDP growth**.
 
• It affects employment as companies downsize to cut costs, leading to an increase in **unemployment rates**.
 
• Recessions often reduce consumer spending and business investment, impacting overall economic stability.
 
• Governments and central banks typically respond to recessions with measures like **stimulus packages** and reduced interest rates to revive economic activity.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Related Terms:**
 
 
• **Inflation:** Refers to the general increase in prices of goods and services over time. Unlike a recession, it signifies economic growth but can lead to reduced purchasing power.
 
• **Reflation:** Describes policy measures taken by governments or central banks to stimulate the economy during a period of stagnation or deflation.
 
• **Stagflation:** A combination of stagnation (slow economic growth) and inflation (rising prices). It is a rare phenomenon and differs from a recession in its economic characteristics.
 
 
 
• **Historical Examples:**
 
 
• The **Great Depression** of the 1930s is one of the most severe recessions in history, caused by stock market crashes and widespread bank failures.
 
• The **2008 Global Financial Crisis** was triggered by the collapse of the housing market and led to a global recession.
 
• The **COVID-19 pandemic** in 2020 caused a recession due to widespread lockdowns and disruptions in economic activity.
 
 
 
• **Important Points:**
 
 
• Recessions are cyclical and often followed by recovery periods where economic activity resumes.
 
• Governments and organizations like the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and **World Bank** play crucial roles in combating and mitigating the effects of recessions.
 
• Tracking economic indicators such as GDP growth, consumer confidence, and unemployment rates can help identify the onset and impact of recessions.

questions.question: Who among the following philosophers and social reformers established the Arya Samaj in 1875?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Swami Dayanand Saraswati**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** founded the **Arya Samaj** on **10 April 1875** in **Bombay (now Mumbai)** to promote the values of the **Vedas** and to reform Indian society.
 
• The Arya Samaj was established to revive the purity of the **Vedic religion** and counteract prevalent social evils such as **caste discrimination**, **child marriage**, and the **practice of Sati**.
 
• Swami Dayanand Saraswati was a strong proponent of **monotheism** and rejected idol worship. His teachings were centered around the ten principles of the Arya Samaj.
 
• He wrote the book **Satyarth Prakash** (The Light of Truth), which became the guiding text of the Arya Samaj, focusing on rational thinking and social reforms.
 
• The Arya Samaj played a significant role in India’s **freedom struggle** and contributed to the spread of **education** and **social awareness** by establishing schools and colleges.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Swami Dayanand Saraswati:**

 
 
• Born on **12 February 1824** in **Tankara, Gujarat**, Swami Dayanand Saraswati was an Indian philosopher and social reformer.
 
• He advocated for the return to the teachings of the **Vedas**, which he believed were the ultimate source of knowledge and truth.
 
• He opposed practices like **idol worship**, **superstitions**, and **ritualistic traditions**, emphasizing rationality and scientific temper.
 
• He coined the phrase **"Back to the Vedas"**, urging people to live life based on the teachings of the Vedas.
 
 
 
• **The Arya Samaj:**
 
 
• The Arya Samaj promoted social reform by campaigning against **untouchability**, encouraging **widow remarriage**, and supporting **education for women**.
 
• It established **Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) schools and colleges** across India to provide modern education blended with Vedic values.
 
• The Arya Samaj was instrumental in the **Shuddhi movement**, which aimed at reconverting people to Hinduism who had converted to other religions.
 
 
 
• **Other Reformers:**
 
 
• **Swami Vivekananda:** A disciple of Ramakrishna Paramahamsa, he founded the **Ramakrishna Mission** and emphasized universal brotherhood and selfless service.
 
• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy:** Known as the "Father of the Indian Renaissance," he founded the **Brahmo Samaj** in 1828 and worked to abolish **Sati** and promote modern education.
 
• **Gopal Krishna Gokhale:** A moderate leader in India’s freedom struggle, he founded the **Servants of India Society** to promote education and social welfare.
 
 
 
• Important Points:
 
 
• The Arya Samaj, under Swami Dayanand Saraswati, played a significant role in the **Indian independence movement** by instilling a sense of nationalism and pride in Indian culture.
 
• It also contributed to the rise of leaders like **Lala Lajpat Rai**, who were deeply influenced by Arya Samaj’s teachings.
 
• The organization continues to function globally, promoting **Vedic teachings** and engaging in **social welfare activities**.

questions.question: The headquarters of NADA (National Anti-Doping Agency), the national organisation which works towards the vision of 'dope free' sports in India, is located in ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**New Delhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA)** is the **apex body** responsible for promoting, coordinating, and monitoring the **anti-doping program** in India.
 
• The headquarters of **NADA** is located in **New Delhi**, the capital city of India, ensuring centralised governance and accessibility.
 
• NADA operates under the **Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports** and works towards the vision of **'dope-free sports'** in India.
 
• It was established in **2009** as part of India’s commitment to the **World Anti-Doping Code** formulated by the **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)**.
 
• The role of NADA includes **education and awareness campaigns** for athletes, conducting **doping tests**, and enforcing penalties for violations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **About New Delhi:**

 
 
• New Delhi is the **capital city of India** and serves as the political and administrative hub of the country.
 
• The city houses major government institutions, including the **President’s Office (Rashtrapati Bhavan)**, Parliament, and **Supreme Court**.
 
• Being centrally located, New Delhi is ideal for hosting the headquarters of national organizations like NADA.
 
• It is also home to several international organizations and embassies.
 
 
 
• **Role and Functions of NADA:**
 
 
• **Testing:** NADA conducts doping tests on athletes during **national and international competitions** and out-of-competition periods.
 
• **Education:** NADA organizes campaigns to **educate athletes** and support staff about the dangers of doping and the importance of clean sports.
 
• **Compliance:** NADA ensures compliance with the **World Anti-Doping Code** and works to implement anti-doping policies in India.
 
• **Enforcement:** It enforces penalties and bans on athletes found guilty of violating anti-doping rules.
 
 
 
• **World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA):**
 
 
• WADA was established in **1999** to promote, coordinate, and monitor the fight against doping in sports globally.
 
• It is headquartered in **Montreal, Canada**, and operates on the principles of the **World Anti-Doping Code**.
 
• India, through NADA, is a signatory to the WADA Code and adheres to its guidelines.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Anti-Doping Efforts:**
 
 
• Ensures **fair competition** among athletes.
 
• Protects the **health and integrity** of athletes by discouraging the use of harmful substances.
 
• Promotes a **clean and ethical sports culture** nationally and globally.

questions.question: Who among the following saints had written the epic 'Mahabharata'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Veda Vyasa**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Veda Vyasa** is traditionally credited with composing the epic **Mahabharata**, which is one of the most significant texts in Indian mythology and history.
 
• He is regarded as a **great sage (Rishi)** in Hindu tradition and is believed to have also compiled the **Vedas**, hence his name "Veda Vyasa."
 
• The **Mahabharata** is written in **Sanskrit** and contains approximately **100,000 verses**, making it one of the longest epic poems in the world.
 
• Veda Vyasa is considered the **central figure** in the Mahabharata, as he not only wrote the epic but also plays a role as a character, appearing in several episodes.
 
• His contributions extend beyond the Mahabharata, as he is also credited with composing the **Puranas** and the **Brahma Sutras**, foundational texts of Hindu philosophy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mahabharata:**

 
 
• The Mahabharata is one of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India, the other being the **Ramayana**.
 
• The epic narrates the story of the Kurukshetra War and the fates of the Kaurava and Pandava princes. It includes significant philosophical and spiritual discourses such as the **Bhagavad Gita**.
 
• The epic is divided into **18 parvas (books)** and covers themes of duty, righteousness, and the consequences of human actions.
 
 
 
• **Role of Veda Vyasa:**
 
 
• Veda Vyasa plays a dual role in the Mahabharata—both as its author and as a character. He is the father of **Dhritarashtra, Pandu, and Vidura**, and is instrumental in the lineage of the Kuru dynasty.
 
• He is also credited with dividing the original Vedas into four parts: **Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, and Atharvaveda**.
 
 
 
• **Other Options Explained:**
 
 
• **Chaitanya:** A saint and religious reformer of Bengal, known for popularizing the Bhakti movement, particularly devotion to Lord Krishna. He did not write the Mahabharata.
 
• **Valmiki:** The author of the epic **Ramayana**, which narrates the story of Lord Rama. Valmiki is not associated with the Mahabharata.
 
• **Ravidas:** A 15th-century saint and poet in the Bhakti movement, known for his devotional songs and verses. He did not write the Mahabharata.
 
 
 
• **Historical and Cultural Significance:**
 
 
• The Mahabharata provides a deep insight into ancient Indian culture, politics, philosophy, and spirituality.
 
• It is considered a **Smriti text** in Hindu tradition, meaning it is remembered and passed down through generations.
 
• The Bhagavad Gita, a part of the Mahabharata, is revered as a sacred scripture and is widely studied for its philosophical teachings.

__
 
• **Malwa**, a region in present-day **Madhya Pradesh**, was conquered by **Ala-ud-din Khalji**, the second ruler of the **Khalji dynasty**, in the year **1305 AD**.
 
• Ala-ud-din Khalji's military campaigns were aimed at expanding the boundaries of the Delhi Sultanate and consolidating his power over central and western India.
